installation.note: lsblk is typically available by default as part of util-linux on most Linux distributions

overview.summary: The lsblk command displays information about block devices (like disks, partitions, and LVM volumes) in a tree-like view. It's commonly used to identify disks, see partition layouts, and find mount points and filesystem types.
when_to_use: Identify which disk/partition corresponds to a device name like /dev/sda1
See what partitions are mounted and where
Troubleshoot storage devices before mounting or formatting

syntax.description: Without a DEVICE, lsblk lists all block devices. You can add options to show filesystems, UUIDs, or choose output columns.

options.description: Show filesystem information (FSTYPE, LABEL, UUID, MOUNTPOINTS)
options.use_case: When you need filesystem types/UUIDs for mounting or fstab
To customize output for scripts or focused troubleshooting

options.description: Print full device paths (e.g., /dev/sda1 instead of sda1)

examples.title: List disks and partitions
examples.description: Show a tree view of block devices with sizes and mount points
examples.output:
NAME   MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda      8:0    0 238.5G  0 disk
├─sda1   8:1    0   512M  0 part /boot/efi
├─sda2   8:2    0     1G  0 part /boot
└─sda3   8:3    0   237G  0 part /
examples.use_case: Figure out what is mounted where and which partition is your root filesystem

examples.title: Show filesystem type and UUID
examples.description: Display filesystem metadata (type/label/UUID) in addition to device layout
examples.use_case: Find a partition's UUID for /etc/fstab entries

common_pitfalls.description: Device names depend on hardware and boot order; they can change between boots, especially with removable drives.
common_pitfalls.solution: Use UUIDs (lsblk -f) in /etc/fstab instead of relying on /dev/sdX names.

related_commands.description: Shows filesystem UUID/label/type details for block devices
